title: Punctuation, Capitalisation and Orthographic Conventions
orientation: Punctuation helps a reader recover structure, reference and relationships. It also follows conventions that vary between publishing systems. This lesson teaches you to separate a genuine boundary error from a legitimate stylistic choice, so that editing improves clarity without overcorrecting standard English. You will practise the full range of practical marks, including quotation, brackets, dashes, hyphens and ellipses, alongside capitals, spelling, dates and abbreviations. Earlier work on clauses, relative structures, reported speech and information structure supplies the grammatical reasoning. The cumulative tasks bring those areas together in notices and edited paragraphs. British English provides the editorial default, but established American forms and other stipulated house styles are identified accurately. For original writing, explain why a mark is present; do not count pauses or apply a blanket rule such as never use a comma before and.
outcomes: Use apostrophes without confusing possession and plurality.
Punctuate quotations and embedded questions by their structure.
Apply a stated spelling and capitalisation policy without rejecting legitimate variants.

modules.title: Clause boundaries, commas and semicolons
modules.definition: Punctuation marks grammatical boundaries and guides interpretation. Some choices repair an incomplete or incorrectly joined structure; others offer legitimate stylistic alternatives. A pause in speech is evidence about rhythm, not a sufficient rule for inserting a comma.
foundation: A full stop normally closes a complete written statement. A comma can separate list items, enclose supplementary material and set off many introductory elements. It does not normally join two independent clauses by itself in formal edited prose: The printer failed, we used another office is a comma splice. Write two sentences, use a semicolon or add a suitable coordinator. Choose the relationship you mean rather than treating all repairs as interchangeable: because introduces a cause, whereas and merely adds information.
intermediate: A semicolon can link closely related independent clauses: The entrance was locked; the caretaker had gone home. A conjunctive adverb such as however does not become a coordinating conjunction. The entrance was locked; however, the side gate remained open is one defensible pattern. A semicolon can also separate complex list items that already contain commas. When an introductory subordinate clause precedes the main clause, a comma is common, particularly if it prevents a misreading. Short introductory adjuncts sometimes appear without one, depending on house style and clarity.
advanced: Commas around a supplementary relative clause are normally paired when the main clause continues: The director, who had just arrived, opened the meeting. A defining relative identifying the intended member ordinarily has no such commas. Punctuation can therefore change reference, not merely rhythm. Do not separate a subject from its verb simply because the subject is long; internal commas may still enclose a parenthetical within that subject. The board, after a long discussion, approved the proposal has two commas performing that enclosing job. A comma before a coordinator may be omitted in short clear clauses or added to prevent confusion.
expert: A punctuation judgement must specify genre and intended analysis. Published literary prose sometimes uses deliberate fragments or comma splices for an identifiable effect; this does not make them a safe default for a formal answer. Conversely, a stylistic comma is not automatically an error. In cumulative editing, first identify every clause and the relation between clauses, then examine marks. A semicolon cannot turn a subordinate fragment into an independent clause. Because the lift was broken; we took the stairs remains faulty for the intended reason relationship. Write Because the lift was broken, we took the stairs instead.

patterns.meaning: Links two complete, closely related statements.
A common clear boundary; short clauses allow some convention-dependent flexibility.

examples.sentence: The results arrived. We checked the totals.
examples.analysis: Two full stops separate complete statements.

examples.sentence: The results arrived, but the annex was missing.
examples.analysis: But coordinates two clauses and expresses contrast.

examples.sentence: The teams came from Multan, Punjab; Sukkur, Sindh; and Quetta, Balochistan.
examples.analysis: Semicolons clarify complex list items containing internal commas.

contrasts.a: The volunteers who had registered received badges.
contrasts.b: The volunteers, who had registered, received badges.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first identifies a subset; the second presents registration as supplementary information about the contextually identified volunteers.

exceptions: A short opening phrase may appear without a comma: In June we moved. Add one when it aids interpretation; do not declare one version universally ungrammatical.

mistakes.problem: The road was flooded, the bus turned back.
mistakes.repair: The road was flooded, so the bus turned back.
mistakes.reason: So explicitly presents a result; a full stop or semicolon can avoid adding a causal claim if none is intended.

mistakes.problem: The documents on the highest shelf, were damaged.
mistakes.repair: The documents on the highest shelf were damaged.
mistakes.reason: The comma wrongly separates the complete subject from its predicate.

glossary.definition: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone in a context requiring a stronger boundary.
A relative clause adding a separate comment about an identified referent.

modules.title: Colons, apostrophes and compact written forms
modules.definition: A colon introduces an explanation, elaboration, list or quotation within an appropriate written structure. An apostrophe marks certain possessive and omitted-letter forms; it is not a general mark of plurality.
foundation: A colon often follows a complete introductory clause: We need three items: a torch, a map and a whistle. Avoid separating an ordinary verb from its required object just to announce a list: The items include: a torch is unnecessary punctuation in continuous prose. Write The items include a torch, a map and a whistle. After the colon, material can be a phrase rather than a full clause. The punctuation signals how that material elaborates the introduction, so a colon differs from a semicolon joining independent clauses.
intermediate: For a singular possessive, a common convention adds apostrophe-s: the writer’s desk. Regular plural possessives ending in s place the apostrophe after that ending: the writers’ desks. Irregular plurals take apostrophe-s: the children’s drawings. Its is possessive without an apostrophe, while it’s contracts it is or it has. Ordinary plurals and dates take no apostrophe: five MPs, the 1990s. Some style guides use apostrophes for single-letter plurals such as dot your i’s; that special convention does not justify writing three file’s.
advanced: Joint and separate relationships need meaning rather than an automatic last-name rule. Ana and Omar’s shared flat presents one jointly held flat; Ana’s and Omar’s separate flats explicitly mark two relationships. Awkward expressions can be recast as the flat shared by Ana and Omar. Singular names ending in s admit house-style variation: James’s notebook and James’ notebook both occur in established editorial systems. Possessive relationships are broader than ownership, as in yesterday’s meeting. Contractions such as don’t and we’ve are grammatical; a formal assignment may prefer uncontracted forms without turning contractions into errors.
expert: Numerals, initials and abbreviations also involve convention. A publication may choose 8 October 2026 or October 8, 2026; apply one consistent system and avoid ambiguous numerical dates where readers use different orders. Dr and Dr. belong to different punctuation conventions, not different standards of intelligence. Introduce an unfamiliar initialism in full before relying on it. The plural normally adds s, while a possessive adds the relevant apostrophe: two NGOs and an NGO’s report. Decimal separators, units and percentage spacing can depend on disciplinary style; preserve a source’s numerical meaning when changing its presentation.

patterns.meaning: The second unit expands or specifies the first.
Marks a possessive relationship involving a regular plural noun.

examples.sentence: One difficulty remained: the missing signature.
examples.analysis: The noun phrase after the colon explains the difficulty.

examples.sentence: The teachers’ comments were attached to the children’s work.
examples.analysis: Teachers is regular plural; children is an irregular plural.

examples.sentence: It’s evident that the NGO has changed its timetable.
examples.analysis: It’s expands to it is, while its is possessive.

contrasts.note: Both possessive spellings are established under different style conventions; choose the stipulated system.

exceptions: Apostrophes in single-letter plurals are allowed by some styles for clarity. Treat that as a limited editorial convention, not a rule for every plural.

mistakes.reason: These are ordinary plurals, not possessives.

mistakes.problem: Its clear that the device has lost it’s settings.
mistakes.repair: It’s clear that the device has lost its settings.
mistakes.reason: The first expression means it is; the second is possessive.

glossary.definition: A grammatical construction often marked by ’s or s’, expressing a relationship.
An abbreviation pronounced as individual letters.

modules.title: Quotation, interruption and sentence-final marks
modules.definition: Quotation marks identify quoted wording or another explicitly defined editorial use. Parentheses, brackets, dashes, hyphens and ellipses do different jobs; none is a general substitute for any inconvenient punctuation.
foundation: A direct question normally ends with a question mark: Has the office reopened? An indirect report normally ends with the mark appropriate to the whole sentence: She asked whether the office had reopened. Do you know whether it has reopened? is itself a question and takes a question mark. An exclamation mark signals an exclamatory expression or emphatic utterance. Multiple exclamation marks occur in informal messages, but restrained formal writing normally avoids them. That preference concerns register; it is not evidence that informal messages must obey a ban on repeated marks.
intermediate: Single or double outer quotation marks can both be used under established styles. When a quotation contains another quotation, switch the inner pair to distinguish levels. Punctuation placement depends partly on whether a mark belongs to the quoted words and partly on the chosen convention. British logical placement and common American practice differ for commas and full stops. Question marks should reflect the intended question: Did she say “Leave now”? asks about the saying; She asked, “May I leave?” quotes a question. Do not add a second full stop mechanically after the closing quotation.
advanced: Round parentheses enclose an aside; square brackets in a quotation commonly identify editorial additions or clarifications. The brackets must not make an uncertain interpretation look like the speaker’s original wording. Dashes can mark interruption, amplification or a strongly separated parenthesis. A hyphen joins elements within some compounds: a three-year project. It is shorter and has a different function from a dash. The need for hyphens varies by position and convention: a well-known author but the author is well known. An -ly adverb normally does not need a hyphen in a clearly written modifier such as a carefully planned route.
expert: An ellipsis can mark an omission from quoted text or a trailing-off effect in an appropriate genre. Omitting words must not change the represented claim. Removing not from a quotation is a substantive distortion even if an ellipsis is printed. A complete omitted sentence and an omitted phrase may be punctuated differently by different style guides; consult the specified guide for the number and spacing of dots. Parenthetical material inside a sentence normally leaves the main sentence’s ending outside the closing parenthesis; a complete independent parenthetical sentence may retain its own final mark inside. Analyse the enclosing structure before choosing the position.

patterns.form: number + unit singular + noun, with a hyphenated modifier
patterns.meaning: A common pattern: a ten-minute break; compare the break lasted ten minutes.

examples.analysis: The question mark belongs to the quoted question.

examples.sentence: The archive closes at six (except on Fridays).
examples.analysis: The parenthesis sits inside the sentence; its full stop follows the closing parenthesis.

examples.sentence: The report described a carefully planned, three-stage operation.
examples.analysis: The -ly modifier has no hyphen; three-stage is a compound premodifier.

contrasts.a: Did he say “The door is locked”?
contrasts.note: The first is an outer question about a statement; the second quotes a question. The question mark follows the relevant structure.

exceptions: Some familiar compounds keep a dictionary hyphen even in positions where other compounds open up. Check a reliable dictionary and the required house style rather than inventing a universal positional rule.

mistakes.problem: She asked whether the office was open?
mistakes.repair: She asked whether the office was open.
mistakes.reason: The whole construction is a statement reporting a question.

mistakes.problem: It was a five years plan.
mistakes.reason: In the compound premodifier, the unit year is singular; a hyphen clarifies the relationship.

glossary.definition: Dots indicating an omission or an appropriate trailing-off effect.
glossary.example: The document states that “the fee … is refundable”.

glossary.definition: A mark joining elements within some compound expressions.

modules.title: Capitalisation, spelling and editorial consistency
modules.definition: Orthography is the system of written forms, including spelling, capitalisation and word division. Some orthographic choices distinguish words; others vary legitimately between national and editorial conventions.
foundation: Capitalise the first word of a normal written sentence, the pronoun I and proper names: Zainab, Pakistan, Urdu and October. A common noun does not become a proper noun merely because it is important: the committee announced the decision is a normal general description. A particular organisation’s official name can require capitals: the National Library. Titles before personal names often receive capitals, while general references often remain lower case. Check whether the wording is an official name, a descriptive phrase or a house-style abbreviation before changing its capitals.
intermediate: British and American spelling conventions differ in words such as colour/color, centre/center and travelled/traveled. Both standard systems are legitimate; this course uses British defaults and identifies American alternatives. British publishing itself permits more than one convention for some words, including forms in -ise and -ize. Do not label every -ize spelling American. Programme is a common British form for a plan or broadcast, while program is standard in computing. A consistent editing policy should still allow quoted material, names and technical forms to retain their authentic spelling.
advanced: Capitalisation of headings and titles varies between sentence case and title case. A sentence-case heading need not capitalise every major word. Institutions and legal publications may prescribe forms such as Section 12, while another style uses section 12 in running prose. Names of languages keep capitals; ordinary names of academic fields often do not unless they form part of an official course title. Compound words may be open, closed or hyphenated, and usage changes over time: a dictionary entry and a publication’s stated style are better evidence than a remembered universal rule.
expert: Separate error correction from editorial normalisation. Writing enviroment for environment is a spelling error; writing organization in a British document may match an established British house style. A question that asks for one correct spelling must avoid offering two standard variants unless it states the convention being tested. Numerical forms also need a stated purpose: scientific prose, dates, tables and literary prose often use different presentation rules. In your final editing pass, check the chosen system, official names, consistency and meaning. Do not remove capitals, hyphens or abbreviations blindly from specialist material merely because the general default differs.

patterns.form: proper name → capitalisation appropriate to the name
patterns.meaning: Distinguishes an identified name from a general description.
Resolves legitimate variants without inventing grammatical prohibitions.

examples.sentence: The department offers courses in chemistry and English.
examples.analysis: English names a language; chemistry is a general field name here.

examples.sentence: The colour of the laboratory’s sign has changed.
examples.analysis: Colour follows the course’s British editorial default.

examples.sentence: The software program supports the festival programme.
examples.analysis: The two forms can coexist under a normal British computing/general distinction.

contrasts.note: Both are standard; the first matches the course’s British spelling default.

exceptions: Official names, quotations and stipulated specialist notation can retain a different convention within an otherwise consistent document.

mistakes.problem: The committee met on monday to discuss urdu teaching.
mistakes.repair: The committee met on Monday to discuss Urdu teaching.
mistakes.reason: The day and language names need capitals.
Environment requires the internal n; this is a spelling correction rather than a national variant.

glossary.definition: The conventional written representation of a language.
A publication’s chosen conventions among available forms.

questions.prompt: Which version is a complete, correctly punctuated sentence in formal edited prose?
questions.why: A semicolon links two independent clauses; the other options contain a comma splice, subordinate fragment or fused boundary.

questions.prompt: The introductory clause gives a reason. Choose the clear standard punctuation.
options: Because the road was closed; we turned back.
Because, the road was closed we turned back.
Because the road was closed, we turned back.
Because the road, was closed we turned back.
questions.why: The comma separates a complete opening reason clause from its main clause; the semicolon cannot make the subordinate clause independent.

questions.prompt: Which form means a lounge used by several teachers?
questions.why: The regular plural teachers takes its possessive apostrophe after s; lounge is singular.

questions.prompt: Choose the genuine error in this sentence: Its clear that the team retained its records.
questions.why: The opening needs It’s, meaning it is. The later possessive its is correct.

questions.prompt: Which sentence itself asks a question?
options: Do you know whether the gate was open?
I wondered whether the gate was open.
She asked whether the gate was open.
The question is whether the gate was open.
questions.why: Only Do you know ...? is an outer interrogative. All embedded clauses retain statement-like subject–verb order.

questions.prompt: Which is a correctly formed compound premodifier?
questions.why: A numerical unit in this compound premodifier uses singular year and a hyphen; the distractors mix plural or possessive structures.

questions.prompt: Which statement about quotation styles is accurate?
options: Nested quotation marks can never be used.
Only double outer quotation marks are grammatical.
Only single outer quotation marks are grammatical.
Single or double outer marks can follow established style conventions.
questions.why: Established styles differ; the chosen outer/inner system should keep quotation levels clear.

questions.prompt: Which is a standard American alternative to the British spelling colour?
questions.why: Color is the established American form. The other options are not the standard alternatives.

questions.prompt: Choose the genuine error: The report—after several revisions—was approved.
questions.why: The paired dashes enclose an aside and the remaining clause is complete; no repair is required.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason not to remove not from a quotation while using an ellipsis?
options: The omission reverses the represented meaning.
An ellipsis can never omit any word.
questions.why: Ellipses may indicate omissions, but the resulting quotation must represent the source faithfully.

questions.prompt: Classify the boundary in The gate was shut, we waited outside, and give one formal repair.
questions.model: It is a comma splice. The gate was shut; we waited outside.
rubric: Use a defensible joining mark or coordinator.
alternatives: Two full sentences or The gate was shut, so we waited outside are valid if the result relation is intended.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference: The workers who were trained used the machine / The workers, who were trained, used the machine.
questions.model: The first identifies the trained subset; the second presents training as supplementary information about the identified workers.
alternatives: Context may establish that the same people happen to be referred to in both versions.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct form of its/it’s: ____ unclear whether the company has changed ____ address.
alternatives: It is may replace the first contraction.

questions.prompt: Insert a colon and apostrophe where needed: One item was missing the directors signature. The signature belongs to one director.
questions.model: One item was missing: the director’s signature.
rubric: Use colon to introduce the explanation.
alternatives: The director’s signature was the one missing item is a grammatical recast.

questions.prompt: Repair: The supplies include: paper, pens and folders.
questions.model: The supplies include paper, pens and folders.
rubric: Do not separate include from its ordinary object list.
alternatives: The supplies include the following items: paper, pens and folders. This retains include without adding a claim that the list is required or exhaustive.

questions.prompt: Arrange and punctuate: had / the meeting / ended / she / asked / whether.
questions.model: She asked whether the meeting had ended.
alternatives: Accept a different response only if it preserves all stated propositions and satisfies the specific instruction, including supplied words, requested construction and sentence count. A grammatical recast that changes those constraints does not complete this task.

questions.prompt: Explain the apostrophes in the children’s teachers’ notes.
questions.model: Children’s is an irregular-plural genitive; teachers’ is a regular-plural genitive.
alternatives: A paraphrase such as notes by the teachers of the children can help explain the nested relationships.

questions.prompt: Compare James’s notebook and James’ notebook as an editor.
questions.model: Both occur in established possessive style systems; choose the assigned house style consistently.
rubric: Do not falsely condemn one form universally.
Identify style as the source of the difference.
alternatives: Recast as the notebook belonging to James if needed.

questions.prompt: Combine using however and suitable boundaries: The archive is open. Its reading room remains closed.
questions.model: The archive is open; however, its reading room remains closed.
rubric: Use a boundary suitable for independent clauses.
alternatives: The archive is open. However, its reading room remains closed is valid.

questions.prompt: Split without losing meaning: The tests were delayed because the laboratory lost power.
questions.model: The laboratory lost power. Because of that, the tests were delayed.
alternatives: Accept a different response only if it preserves all stated propositions and satisfies the specific instruction, including supplied words, requested construction and sentence count. A grammatical recast that changes those constraints does not complete this task.

questions.prompt: In The chair, after consulting the members, adjourned the meeting, why is the comma before adjourned acceptable?
questions.model: It closes the parenthetical after consulting the members; it does not stand alone between the subject and verb.
rubric: Recover The chair adjourned the meeting.
alternatives: A pair of dashes or no parenthetical placement can also express the structure.

questions.prompt: Turn the duration into a compound modifier: The break lasted ten minutes. It was a ____ break.
rubric: Use singular minute inside the compound.
alternatives: Accept a different response only if it preserves all stated propositions and satisfies the specific instruction, including supplied words, requested construction and sentence count. A grammatical recast that changes those constraints does not complete this task.

questions.prompt: Explain the question-mark position: Did Mina say “The office is shut”? / Mina asked, “Is the office shut?”
questions.model: The first question belongs to the enclosing clause; the second belongs to the quoted words.
rubric: Relate the mark to that interrogative.
alternatives: Equivalent explicit structural explanations are valid.

questions.prompt: Edit for a conventional formal reading: the results arrived, we checked them. Its clear that two report’s are missing.
questions.model: The results arrived; we checked them. It’s clear that two reports are missing.
rubric: Correct it’s and ordinary plural reports.
alternatives: A full stop or coordinator is also a valid first-boundary repair.

questions.prompt: What does the colon do in Only one objection remained: the cost?
questions.model: It introduces a noun phrase explaining the objection.
rubric: Do not require a full clause after the colon.
alternatives: Elaboration/specification is an appropriate functional label.

questions.prompt: Why is replacing colour with color not the same kind of correction as replacing enviroment with environment?
questions.model: Colour/color are standard national alternatives; enviroment is a misspelling of environment.
rubric: State the editorial default without mislabelling the alternative.
alternatives: A publication may normalise spelling to its chosen system.

questions.prompt: Write a two-sentence announcement using a date, an initialism introduced in full and one possessive.
questions.model: The Community Reading Group (CRG) will meet on 8 November 2026. The group’s secretary will circulate the agenda.
rubric: Use an unambiguous date and a defensible possessive.
alternatives: Other original announcements meeting the constraints are valid.

questions.prompt: A quotation says The proposal is not supported. A writer quotes it as “The proposal is … supported.” Diagnose the problem.
questions.model: The omitted not reverses the claim; the ellipsis does not make the quotation faithful.
alternatives: Retain not or paraphrase with accurate attribution.

corrections.prompt: Repair: The workers who arrived before noon, received badges.
corrections.model: The workers who arrived before noon received badges.
alternatives: A supplementary reading would require a different paired-comma analysis.

corrections.prompt: Repair: The office closed, however, the helpline remained open.
corrections.model: The office closed; however, the helpline remained open.
rubric: Use a full boundary before however.
alternatives: A full stop before However is valid.

corrections.prompt: Repair: The childrens drawings filled three wall’s.
corrections.model: The children’s drawings filled three walls.
alternatives: Drawings by the children filled three walls is valid.

corrections.prompt: No change if grammatical: The research, although incomplete, is useful.
alternatives: Although incomplete, the research is useful is a valid recast.

corrections.prompt: Repair: She wondered where was the receipt?
corrections.model: She wondered where the receipt was.
rubric: End the reporting statement with a full stop.
alternatives: She wondered, “Where is the receipt?” would be direct thought quotation with a different presentation.

corrections.prompt: Repair: It is a carefully-planned two days workshop.
corrections.model: It is a carefully planned, two-day workshop.
rubric: Use singular day and a hyphen in two-day.
alternatives: It is a carefully planned two-day workshop is valid without the optional separating comma.

corrections.prompt: The institution’s official name is National Library. Correct capitals only in: “on tuesday, sara will teach english at the national library.”
corrections.model: On Tuesday, Sara will teach English at the National Library.
rubric: Capitalise sentence, day, person and language.
Use capitals for the supplied official name.
alternatives: A different sentence arrangement preserving these names is valid.

corrections.prompt: No change if grammatical under a style using American spelling: The center has changed its program.
rubric: Accept the stated standard spelling convention.
Do not insert an apostrophe into possessive its.
alternatives: A British editorial version may use centre and, for a non-computing programme, programme.

transformations.prompt: Join with a colon without adding information: We need one document. The document is your signed declaration.
transformations.model: We need one document: your signed declaration.
rubric: Use the second noun phrase as elaboration.
alternatives: Accept a different response only if it preserves all stated propositions and satisfies the specific instruction, including supplied words, requested construction and sentence count. A grammatical recast that changes those constraints does not complete this task.

transformations.prompt: Recast to remove the awkward joint possessive without changing joint ownership: Farah and Bilal’s shared office is upstairs.
transformations.model: The office shared by Farah and Bilal is upstairs.
alternatives: Farah and Bilal share an upstairs office is valid.

writing.prompt: Write a 90–120-word notice about a fictional community workshop. Include a date, a list, a supplementary clause, one direct quotation containing a question, and one possessive. Then identify which punctuation choices follow grammar and which follow your chosen house style.
writing.model:
The community workshop will take place on 18 November at the village hall. Participants should bring three items: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler. The organiser, who will open the hall at nine, asks everyone to arrive ten minutes before the first demonstration. “Which tools will we use?” a participant asked during registration. The tutor’s reply will be included in the confirmation message, together with a short safety checklist. Please tell the organiser about any access requirements before the event. The booking record will remain open until the room reaches its stated capacity.

Analysis: Sentence boundaries and paired supplementary commas reflect the constructions. The possessive tutor’s identifies one tutor. Double outer quotation marks and the day–month date follow the chosen house style; an established consistent single-quotation style is also legitimate. The colon follows a complete introduction to a list.
rubric: Use complete sentence boundaries and matched supplementary punctuation.
Include the specified meaningful forms without inventing contradictory facts.
Explain a legitimate quotation/list/date style choice.
Judge original writing against the rubric, not exact model wording.
alternatives: Different notices and established punctuation systems are valid when consistently applied.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 21: Why does Do you know where the records are? take a question mark while He asked where the records were. takes a full stop?
recall.model: The first whole sentence is an interrogative; the second is a statement reporting an embedded question.
rubric: Keep embedded order distinct from punctuation.
alternatives: Equivalent whole-sentence explanations are valid.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 19: Repair The bridge has repaired and reopened. The intended meaning is that workers have completed both actions on it.
recall.model: The bridge has been repaired and reopened.
rubric: Use perfect passive has been + participles.
alternatives: Workers have repaired and reopened the bridge is valid.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 23: Why does Only after the inspection had ended did we leave use did before we?
recall.model: The fronted restrictive adjunct licenses subject–auxiliary inversion in the main clause.
alternatives: We left only after the inspection had ended is a valid neutral-order equivalent.

checklist: I can explain each major sentence boundary.
I check paired punctuation rather than isolated commas.
I distinguish a plural from a genitive.
I identify a quoted question and the outer sentence separately.
I can state my editorial convention.
